body:
From political associations to mass participation

During the late nineteenth century, much of the organised nationalist movement was led by educated professionals, journalists and political associations. The Indian National Congress, established in 1885, gradually developed a wider programme against British rule. After 1919, the struggle increasingly involved peasants, tribal communities, industrial workers, students, women and socially disadvantaged groups.

This expansion is called mass nationalism. It meant that people who had previously remained outside formal political organisations began participating in protests, boycotts, strikes and local campaigns. However, participation did not mean that everyone had the same demands or followed the same leaders.

Why different groups joined

Colonial policies affected different sections of Indian society in different ways. A cultivator might be concerned about land revenue, while a factory worker might demand higher wages. A tribal community might oppose restrictions on forest use, while students might object to colonial control over education.

  • Peasants: High land revenue, excessive rent, indebtedness, eviction and forced cultivation of commercial crops were important grievances.
  • Tribal and forest communities: Forest restrictions, loss of customary land rights, demands for unpaid labour and exploitation by traders and moneylenders encouraged resistance.
  • Industrial and plantation workers: Low wages, long working hours, harsh treatment and restrictions on movement shaped their demands.
  • Women: Nationalist campaigns offered opportunities for public action, while women's organisations also demanded education, political rights and social reform.
  • Students: Boycotting colonial educational institutions, establishing national schools and organising demonstrations became important forms of participation.
  • Dalits and other marginalised communities: Struggles for social equality, access to public facilities and independent political representation accompanied the demand for national freedom.

What did swaraj mean?

Swaraj broadly meant self-rule. In the national movement, it expressed opposition to foreign domination. Yet its practical meaning differed among participants. For many peasants, freedom also meant relief from oppressive landlords or revenue demands. For Assam tea plantation workers, it could mean the freedom to leave the plantation and return to their villages. For Dalit leaders, political freedom without an end to caste discrimination was insufficient.

The Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920–1922 encouraged people to withdraw support from colonial institutions through boycotts, resignations and the rejection of foreign goods. The Civil Disobedience Movement beginning in 1930 went further by deliberately breaking particular colonial laws, especially the salt law. Local groups connected these national programmes with their own grievances.

Participation in a national movement did not automatically make every local protest a Congress-led or Gandhian movement. Some organisations worked independently, and some adopted methods that Gandhi or the Congress leadership opposed.

Leadership and unequal participation

Mass movements depended on village organisers, local associations, volunteers and women who arranged meetings, carried messages, collected contributions or maintained protests. Nevertheless, access to leadership was unequal. Caste, gender, property, education and regional conditions influenced who could speak publicly, hold office or make political decisions.

Prelims focus

  • The Indian National Congress was established in 1885.
  • The Non-Cooperation Movement became a major mass campaign in 1920–1922.
  • The Civil Disobedience Movement began in 1930 with the Salt Satyagraha.
  • Peasant, tribal, labour, student and women's movements had different immediate objectives.
  • Trap: Swaraj did not have an identical practical meaning for every participating group.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21 edition, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 109–119; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed pp. 57–69.]

title: The Indian National Movement as a Mass Movement

body:
How colonial agriculture created grievances

Peasants cultivated land under different arrangements. Some held land directly and paid land revenue to the colonial state. Others cultivated land belonging to landlords and paid rent. Many borrowed money to obtain seeds, tools or food, and some were compelled to grow crops required by European markets.

These distinctions are important because different peasant movements targeted different forms of exploitation. A protest against a moneylender was not necessarily a demand to reduce government land revenue.

The Indigo Revolt, 1859–1860

In Bengal, European indigo planters pressured cultivators to grow indigo, a plant used to produce blue dye. Under the ryoti system, planters advanced loans to cultivators who agreed, often under pressure, to produce indigo on part of their holdings. Cultivators received low prices, remained trapped in debt and lost the opportunity to grow food crops on their best land.

In 1859, large numbers of Bengal peasants refused to grow indigo. The resistance spread during 1859–1860 and included refusal of cultivation, collective protest and attacks on some planter establishments. Women also participated. The colonial government appointed an Indigo Commission in 1860 to investigate the system.

The central issue was forced commercial cultivation and planter exploitation, not a campaign for a separate national government. The revolt demonstrated that cultivators could organise collectively against powerful economic interests.

The Pabna Agrarian Unrest, beginning in 1873

In the Pabna district of eastern Bengal, tenants opposed landlords who attempted to increase rents, impose unlawful cesses and weaken their occupancy rights. In May 1873, cultivators formed an agrarian league in the Yusufshahi area.

The movement raised funds for legal proceedings, held public meetings and organised resistance to enhanced rent. Legal action and organised non-payment of disputed increases were important features. Unlike the Indigo Revolt, the immediate dispute was mainly between tenants and zamindars over rent and tenancy rights.

The Deccan Riots, 1875

In western India, many cultivators depended on moneylenders, commonly called sahukars. Debt increased because of high revenue obligations, agricultural difficulties and unfavourable credit arrangements. Moneylenders could use written bonds and account books to enforce claims against debtors.

On 12 May 1875, cultivators attacked moneylenders at Supa in the Poona district. The unrest spread into parts of Poona and Ahmednagar. Protesters demanded debt documents, destroyed account books and bonds, and attacked some moneylenders' property.

The symbolic importance of destroying debt records was clear: cultivators believed that these documents were instruments through which moneylenders maintained control over them. The revolt was directed primarily at rural indebtedness and creditor power.

Three movements, three principal targets

MovementArea and yearPrincipal grievance
Indigo RevoltBengal, 1859–1860Forced indigo cultivation and planter exploitation
Pabna Agrarian UnrestEastern Bengal, from 1873Enhanced rent and insecure tenancy
Deccan RiotsPoona and Ahmednagar, 1875Debt and moneylender control

These movements preceded Gandhi's major Indian campaigns. They should be understood as important forms of rural resistance in their own right, even when their immediate demands were not framed as a struggle for complete national independence.

Prelims focus

  • Indigo Revolt: Bengal, 1859–1860; opposition to European indigo planters.
  • Pabna Agrarian League: formed in 1873 in the Yusufshahi area of Bengal.
  • Deccan Riots: began at Supa in the Poona district on 12 May 1875.
  • Indigo Commission: appointed in 1860.
  • Trap: Pabna chiefly concerned tenant-landlord relations; the Deccan Riots chiefly targeted moneylenders.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21 edition, chapter Ruling the Countryside, printed pp. 27–38; NCERT, Themes in Indian History–Part III, Class 12, chapter Colonialism and the Countryside, section 3.1, Account Books Are Burnt, as reproduced by IIT Kanpur SATHEE, consulted 22 November 2026; IGNOU, Land Reforms in Independent India, Unit 1, section Pabna Agrarian Unrest (1873–76), consulted 22 November 2026.]

title: Early Peasant Resistance: Indigo, Rent and Rural Debt

body:
Peasant grievances enter Gandhian mass politics

Gandhi's early interventions in India connected local economic grievances with satyagraha, a method of resistance based on truth, non-violence and willingness to suffer rather than inflict violence. The campaigns in Champaran, Kheda and Bardoli are important because they involved different agricultural problems and different leadership arrangements.

Champaran Satyagraha, 1917

In Champaran, Bihar, indigo cultivators opposed the oppressive arrangements imposed by European planters. The well-known tinkathia system required indigo cultivation on 3 out of every 20 parts of a holding under the prevailing arrangement. Gandhi's intervention in 1917 helped bring the cultivators' grievances into public discussion and official investigation.

Champaran concerned indigo cultivation and planter control. It should not be confused with a movement against an increase in government land revenue.

Kheda Satyagraha, 1918

In Kheda district, Gujarat, poor harvest conditions made it difficult for cultivators to pay land revenue. Gandhi, Vallabhbhai Patel and other local organisers supported a campaign for relief from the revenue demand in 1918.

Peasants who could not afford payment were encouraged to resist collection non-violently. The central demand was suspension or remission of land revenue in a period of agricultural distress. Kheda thus differed from Champaran in both its immediate cause and the authority being challenged.

Bardoli Satyagraha, 1928

In Bardoli taluka of Surat district, Gujarat, the colonial administration decided to raise the land revenue assessment by 22% overall, with higher increases proposed for some villages. Cultivators considered the assessment unjustified.

At a conference on 12 February 1928, they decided to withhold land revenue under the leadership of Vallabhbhai Patel. The government responded with property seizures and other coercive measures, but the organised campaign continued. An inquiry followed, and the increased assessment was substantially reduced. Patel acquired the popular title Sardar through his leadership in this struggle.

Awadh peasants and the Oudh Kisan Sabha

In Awadh, peasants faced excessive rent, additional cesses, eviction and begar, meaning labour demanded without payment. Baba Ramchandra, who had previously worked as an indentured labourer in Fiji, became an important organiser.

Jawaharlal Nehru visited villages in Awadh in 1920. In October 1920, the Oudh Kisan Sabha was established under the leadership of Nehru, Baba Ramchandra and others. Village branches spread rapidly.

Peasants demanded reduced burdens, protection from eviction and an end to begar. Some groups used nai-dhobi bandhs, a social boycott in which barbers and washermen withdrew services from oppressive landlords. As agitation spread in 1921, attacks on landlords and merchants also occurred. Such actions went beyond Gandhi's prescribed method of non-violent protest.

Why rich and poor peasants responded differently in 1930

The worldwide economic depression reduced agricultural prices and cultivators' cash incomes. Under these conditions, different rural groups joined the Civil Disobedience Movement for different reasons.

  • Relatively prosperous cultivators: Communities such as the Patidars of Gujarat and Jats of Uttar Pradesh were affected by falling crop prices while the government's revenue demands remained high. They supported refusal to pay land revenue.
  • Poor tenants: Many cultivated land rented from landlords. Their central demand was relief from rent owed to landlords, including the remission of unpaid rent.

The Congress leadership generally hesitated to endorse extensive no-rent campaigns because these could alienate landlords and relatively prosperous cultivators within the nationalist coalition. Many prosperous peasants were also disappointed when the movement was suspended in 1931 without the expected reduction in revenue.

No revenue meant refusing payment demanded by the state. No rent meant refusing payment owed to a landlord. The distinction identifies both the demand and the party against whom the protest was directed.

Prelims focus

  • Champaran, 1917: indigo cultivators and European planters.
  • Kheda, 1918: crop distress and land revenue relief in Gujarat.
  • Oudh Kisan Sabha, October 1920: associated with Baba Ramchandra and Jawaharlal Nehru.
  • Bardoli, 1928: Vallabhbhai Patel; proposed 22% revenue assessment increase.
  • Patidars of Gujarat and Jats of Uttar Pradesh supported Civil Disobedience over revenue grievances.
  • Trap: The immediate demands of prosperous peasant proprietors and poor tenants were not identical.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21 edition, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 115–119; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed pp. 58–59 and 65–66; Indian National Congress, biographical account Vallabhbhai J. Patel, Bardoli Satyagraha section, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Champaran, Kheda and Bardoli addressed different agrarian grievances.

title: Peasant Satyagrahas, Kisan Mobilisation and the Civil Disobedience Movement

body:
Why peasants formed their own organisations

Local peasant protests often began in response to a particular tax, rent demand or landlord practice. Over time, organisers sought more permanent institutions that could represent cultivators beyond a single village or district. These institutions were generally known as Kisan Sabhas, meaning peasant associations.

A Kisan Sabha could organise meetings, communicate demands, resist eviction or excessive rent, and coordinate protests. Such organisations sometimes cooperated with the Congress, but they also developed independent programmes. Congress Socialists, Communists and other agrarian activists became influential in several areas.

Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha, 1929

Swami Sahajanand Saraswati became a major organiser of peasants in Bihar. The Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha was established at Sonepur in November 1929, with Sahajanand as its first president.

The organisation challenged exploitation by landlords and sought stronger protection for tenants and cultivators. It provided an important provincial base for the growth of an all-India peasant movement.

All India Kisan Sabha, 1936

The first All India Kisan Congress met at Lucknow on 11 April 1936. The organisation subsequently became known as the All India Kisan Sabha (AIKS).

Swami Sahajanand Saraswati was its first president and N. G. Ranga its first general secretary. It brought together activists from provincial peasant organisations, including Congress Socialists, Communists and other leaders concerned with agrarian grievances.

Its demands included relief from landlord exploitation and changes in agrarian relations. The organisation's significance lay in attempting to connect local rural struggles through an all-India peasant platform.

The Oudh Kisan Sabha of 1920, the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha of 1929 and the All India Kisan Sabha formed in 1936 were not the same organisation. Their names, regional reach and founding dates must be distinguished.

The Tebhaga Movement, 1946–1947

In Bengal, many cultivators were bargadars or sharecroppers. They cultivated land belonging to another person and gave the landholder a share of the harvest. Under a common arrangement, the crop was divided equally between the sharecropper and the landholder.

In 1946, the Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha supported the Tebhaga Movement. Its central demand was that the sharecropper should retain 2/3 of the harvest, leaving 1/3 for the landholder. The movement continued into 1947.

The word tebhaga refers to division into 3 parts. It concerned the distribution of agricultural produce, not a demand for a general 2/3 reduction in government land revenue.

The Telangana peasant struggle from 1946

In the Telangana region of Hyderabad State, peasants opposed oppressive landlords, forced labour and feudal exactions. A major peasant struggle began in 1946, with important participation by Communist-led organisers.

The Telangana movement differed from Tebhaga. Tebhaga centred on the division of produce between sharecroppers and landholders in Bengal. Telangana involved wider struggles over landlord domination, land rights and forced labour. The Telangana struggle continued beyond India's independence in 1947.

Regional and class differences

Peasant organisations did not represent every rural group equally. Landholding cultivators, tenants, sharecroppers and landless agricultural workers had overlapping but distinct interests. For example, a cultivator seeking lower government revenue might still employ agricultural labourers, whose main concerns were wages and working conditions.

Prelims focus

  • Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha: Sonepur, 1929; Swami Sahajanand Saraswati.
  • First All India Kisan Congress: Lucknow, 11 April 1936.
  • All India Kisan Sabha: first president Sahajanand Saraswati; first general secretary N. G. Ranga.
  • Tebhaga Movement: Bengal, 1946–1947; demand for 2/3 of the harvest for sharecroppers.
  • Telangana peasant struggle: began in Hyderabad State in 1946 and continued after independence.
  • Trap: Tebhaga concerned crop sharing, not the abolition of all agricultural rent.

[Sources: Prime Ministers Museum and Library, Institutional Collections, section Peasant Movements and All India Kisan Sabha, and collection on Sahajanand Saraswati, consulted 22 November 2026; Prime Ministers Museum and Library, Agrarian Issues, Peasant Movements, and the Congress Politics in Bihar, 1929–1950, section Formation of Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha, consulted 22 November 2026; V. V. Giri National Labour Institute, The Agony and the Hope: Indian Agricultural Labour, discussion of All India Kisan Sabha, consulted 22 November 2026; Babu P. Remesh, A Struggle for Fair Share: Recounting the Tebhaga Movement, 1946–47, Labour File, vol. 9, issue 2, 2014, consulted 22 November 2026.]
